primary_claim: A linear probe on Qwen2.5-1.5B activations reads a small model's internal, never-transcribed automaton state (a 6-state login DFA) correctly 88.6% of the time and outperforms order-blind baselines on order-ambiguous positions (80.8% vs 60.4% max), but the model cannot represent the count needed to distinguish 'two failures' from 'locked' (chance-level, ~50%, at every layer, even when the three-strikes rule is stated), and split-half probe testing confirms these are genuine model limitations rather than probe artifacts (only 33.8% agreement between two independently trained probes on the original probe's errors)

effect.metric: linear probe classification accuracy on internal automaton state
effect.value: 88.6% overall (vs 76.9% transcript-only, 20% majority baseline); 80.8% on order-ambiguous positions (vs 60.4% max for order-blind methods); 50.8% on the 'two failures' vs 'locked' distinction (chance)

stated_future_work: test whether bigger models keep count
test how well the model internally keeps states on messier harnesses based on more complicated real-life scenarios
causal tests to separate 'this state is usable' from 'this state is readable'
explore whether long-running agents gravitate toward the 'locked' (absorbing) state more as the transcript goes on
limitations_stated: tested on a single model and a single DFA design
the planned experiment testing whether the model would fall for a tempting task while believing it was in the 'two failures' state never ran ('never saw the light of day')
linear probes cannot by themselves distinguish a model that encodes a faulty count from a probe that is guessing; required a separate split-half reliability check to resolve
quote: The state is correctly read from the model's activation 88.6% of the time... Any method that sees the events and their number, but not their order, gets a maximum of 60.4%, but the probe scores 80.8% here.
